chief_complaint: severe crushing chest pain after violent retching and vomiting following heavy alcohol consumption
hpi_details: 46M brought by EMS after waking with severe nausea after drinking 1.5 liters of whiskey. Experienced prolonged, violent retching and vomiting, followed suddenly by excruciating, burning left-sided chest and upper abdominal pain radiating to his left shoulder and back. Reports feeling faint and diaphoretic.

concerns: worried because every breath causes agonizing stabbing chest pain
expectations: wants strong pain relief and immediate diagnosis

clinical_knowledge.topic: Boerhaave Syndrome (Spontaneous Esophageal Rupture) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Boerhaave Syndrome (Spontaneous Esophageal Rupture) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes STAT cardiothoracic/thoracic surgical emergency: immediate transfer to operating room for left posterolateral thoracotomy, primary repair of esophageal tear with pleural/intercostal muscle flap buttress, thorough wide debridement and decortication of mediastinum and pleural space, and placement of large-bore chest drainage tubes, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: severe crushing chest pain after violent retching and vomiting following heavy alcohol consumption

Key HPI features: 46M brought by EMS after waking with severe nausea after drinking 1.5 liters of whiskey. Experienced prolonged, violent retching and vomiting, followed suddenly by excruciating, burning left-sided chest and upper abdominal pain radiating to his left shoulder and back. Reports feeling faint and diaphoretic.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: HR 124, BP 90/58, RR 26, Temp 38.3C. Palpable crepitus (subcutaneous emphysema) over left lower anterior chest wall and neck (Hamman crunch audible on cardiac auscultation during systole). Chest X-ray and CT chest with water-soluble oral contrast (Gastrografin) demonstrate a full-thickness rupture of the left posterolateral distal esophagus (Boerhaave syndrome) with leakage of contrast into the left pleural cavity, pneumomediastinum, and a large left hydropneumothorax with mediastinitis.
Relevant background/PMH: Alcohol use disorder, Gastroesophageal reflux disease
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Boerhaave Syndrome (Spontaneous Esophageal Rupture).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Myocardial infarction without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Pain immediately following forceful vomiting/retching — the classic trigger for this diagnosis.
management_principles: Urgent thoracic surgical emergency: operative or endoscopic management is selected according to stability, time since perforation, contamination, and local expertise; provide source control and wide drainage when indicated
Start broad-spectrum IV antibacterial therapy promptly; add antifungal therapy selectively based on risk factors, cultures, and local guidance
Strict NPO with feeding jejunostomy placement
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 46M presenting with Mackler triad of Boerhaave syndrome: heavy binge drinking, violent retching/vomiting, and sudden severe thoracic pain with subcutaneous emphysema.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals: HR 124, BP 90/58, RR 26, Temp 38.3C. Palpable crepitus (subcutaneous emphysema) over left lower anterior chest wall and neck (Hamman crunch audible on cardiac auscultation during systole). Chest X-ray and CT chest with water-soluble oral contrast (Gastrografin) demonstrate a full-thickness rupture of the left posterolateral distal esophagus (Boerhaave syndrome) with leakage of contrast into the left pleural cavity, pneumomediastinum, and a large left hydropneumothorax with mediastinitis.
reference_soap.assessment: Boerhaave Syndrome (Spontaneous Transmural Esophageal Perforation) with acute bacterial and chemical mediastinitis.
reference_soap.plan: Urgent thoracic surgical emergency: operative or endoscopic management is selected according to stability, time since perforation, contamination, and local expertise; provide source control and wide drainage when indicated. Start broad-spectrum IV antibacterial therapy promptly; add antifungal therapy selectively based on risk factors, cultures, and local guidance. Keep the patient strictly NPO and establish enteral access when appropriate.

learning_objectives: Recognize Mackler's Triad of Boerhaave Syndrome (vomiting, lower thoracic pain, subcutaneous emphysema) and Hamman's crunch
Understand why water-soluble contrast esophagography or CT is generally used first, with barium contrast considered when needed after a negative initial study because it can improve leak detection
Explain the critical relationship between time to surgical intervention (<24 hours vs >24 hours) and mortality in esophageal perforation
Outline operative principles of primary esophageal repair, tissue buttressing, and wide drainage of contaminated mediastinal spaces

teaching.one_liner: Forceful vomiting causes a full-thickness tear of the esophagus, spilling gastric contents into the mediastinum and causing severe chest and back pain with rapidly developing infection — a surgical emergency.
red_flags: Pain immediately following forceful vomiting/retching — the classic trigger for this diagnosis

must_ask.say: Did the chest pain start right after the vomiting and retching?
How much did you drink before this happened?
Where is the pain, and does it spread to your shoulder or back?
Does every breath make the pain worse?
Do you feel faint or sweaty?
